title: Managing breaking changes across branches
description: Learn about Managing breaking changes across branches. Master the concepts, patterns, and best practices.

data.text: Managing breaking changes across branches requires communication, versioning discipline, and incremental migration. A breaking change is any modification that removes or alters existing behavior in a way that can cause client code to fail.

data.title: Lesson Scope
data.text: This lesson covers semantic versioning, deprecation warnings, API versioning, database migration strategies, and coordinating breaking changes across multiple branches.
Advanced Breaking-Change Practices
The sections below go deeper into the mechanics of shipping breaking changes: deprecation policy, API versioning, database migrations, and contract testing.
Types of Breaking Changes

items: Removing a public API endpoint
Changing a function signature in a library
Renaming a database column without a migration
Modifying the shape of a JSON response
Removing or renaming a configuration option
Changing default behavior that callers relied upon

data.text: Semantic Versioning Deep Dive
Semantic versioning encodes the impact of changes in a version number: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. A breaking change increments the major version, signaling that clients must review migration steps.
Pre-Versioning Considerations
Before version 1.0.0, you are not bound by strict SemVer rules. However, treating early versions as if they were stable helps build good habits and avoids surprising early adopters.

items: Document what is stable and what is experimental
Communicate API changes even before 1.0.0
Use changelogs to track evolution
Consider early adopters when making breaking changes

data.text: Deprecation Policy
Define a deprecation policy in your CONTRIBUTING guide. State how long deprecated features remain available and how they are communicated to users.

data.title: Deprecation Policy Template
data.code:
## Deprecation Policy

We aim to provide at least one minor release of notice before removing deprecated features.

1. Deprecation warning is added in release X.Y.Z
2. Feature is removed in release X.(Y+2).0
3. Migration guide is published alongside the deprecation

data.text: Runtime Deprecation Warnings
Issue warnings at runtime when deprecated APIs are used. This gives consumers immediate feedback without waiting for them to read the changelog.

data.title: Runtime Deprecation Warning

data.text: Deprecation Logging
Log deprecation usage to a metrics system. This helps you understand how many consumers are still using the deprecated API and when it is safe to remove it.

data.title: Deprecation Metrics
data.code:
metrics.increment('deprecation.legacyParse');

# Dashboard shows how many requests still use the old path

data.text: Feature Flags for Breaking Changes
Feature flags let you ship breaking code paths behind a toggle. Old behavior remains active while new behavior is validated. Once confidence is high, flip the flag and eventually remove the old code.

data.title: Feature Flag Lifecycle

data.text: API Versioning Strategies
Versioning APIs through the URL or headers lets you introduce breaking changes without disrupting existing clients. Choose a strategy that fits your routing, caching, and client ecosystem.

cards.title: Header
cards.description: Accept: application/vnd.example.v2+json. Clean URLs but requires client support.

data.text: Content Negotiation
Content negotiation lets clients request a specific version via the Accept header. This keeps URLs clean while allowing version-specific responses.

data.title: Content Negotiation Example

data.text: Parallel API Versions
Run multiple API versions in parallel during a migration. Each version has its own route handlers, validation, and tests. This reduces risk and gives consumers a gradual upgrade path.

items: Deploy v1 and v2 side by side
Route requests based on URL or header
Monitor v2 adoption rate
Deprecate v1 when adoption is sufficient

data.text: Database Migration Patterns
Database changes are among the most dangerous breaking changes. Use expand-contract or parallel-write patterns to migrate data without downtime.

items: Expand: Add the new column or table alongside the old one. Write to both.
Migrate: Backfill existing data from old to new.
Contract: Remove reads and writes from the old column. Drop it later.
Repeat: Allow one full release cycle between each step.

data.title: Expand-Contract Migration

data.text: Online Schema Changes
For large tables, use online schema change tools such as pt-online-schema-change or gh-ost. These tools create a shadow table, copy data in chunks, and swap tables with minimal downtime.
Feature Flags and Database Changes
Combine feature flags with database migrations for maximum safety. Deploy the new column and code path behind a flag, then enable the flag gradually.

items: Add new column alongside old one
Deploy code that writes to both columns
Enable flag for internal users
Enable flag for external users
Drop old column in a later release

data.text: Backward Compatibility
Aim for backward-compatible changes whenever possible. Adding optional fields, adding new endpoints, or extending enums are usually safe. Removing or renaming requires a deprecation cycle.

cards.title: Safe
cards.description: Add optional field, new endpoint, extend enum.

cards.title: Breaking
cards.description: Remove endpoint, rename field, change type without conversion.

data.text: Contract Testing
Contract tests verify that APIs meet their specified interface. Use them to catch breaking changes before they reach production. Pact and Spring Cloud Contract are popular tools.

data.title: Pact Contract Test

data.text: Consumer-Driven Contracts
Consumer-driven contracts are written by API consumers. They specify what data they expect from the provider. If the provider breaks the contract, the build fails before production.

items: Consumers write tests that specify their expectations
Provider runs consumer tests against their API
Breaking changes are caught in CI
Consumers and providers agree on contract versions

data.text: Coordinating Across Branches

When multiple feature branches depend on shared APIs, a breaking change in one branch can break another. Communicate the change early, define a migration window, and use feature branches or flags to integrate safely.

items: Announce breaking changes in the team channel before merging
Open a tracking issue for the migration work
Update dependent branches to use the new API before merging
Keep the old API available until all consumers migrate

data.text: Migration Tracking Issue

data.title: Migration Tracking Issue
data.code:
## Migrate to v2 Auth API

### Affected Services
- [ ] web-frontend
- [ ] mobile-api
- [ ] admin-portal

### Deadline
2026-10-15

### Owner
@platform-team

data.text: Branching Strategy for Breaking Changes
Some teams create a dedicated migration branch for breaking changes. The migration branch updates all consumers, and once every service compiles and passes tests, the branch is merged.

data.title: Migration Branch Workflow
data.code:
git checkout -b migration/v2-auth-api main

# Update all consumers to new API
# Run integration tests

# Merge back to main when green
git checkout main
git merge --no-ff migration/v2-auth-api

data.text: Rollback Plans
Every breaking change should have a documented rollback plan. If the new behavior causes unexpected failures, the team must know how to revert quickly or fall back to the old behavior.

items: Keep old code paths available behind a feature flag
Tag releases so you can deploy a previous version
Prepare database rollback scripts alongside forward migrations
Run post-deploy smoke tests to catch regressions early

data.text: Testing Breaking Changes
Write integration tests that cover both old and new behavior during the transition period. Contract tests between services help detect breaking API changes before they reach production.

data.title: Contract Test Example

data.text: Documentation Updates
Update documentation in the same pull request as the breaking change. Do not leave the docs stale while the code moves forward.

data.title: Migration Guide Structure
data.code:
# Migrating to v2 Auth

## Before
GET /api/v1/auth?token=...

## After
POST /api/v2/auth
Body: { "refreshToken": "..." }

## Step-by-Step
1. Replace GET with POST
2. Move token from query to body
3. Handle new response shape

data.text: Summary

Breaking changes are inevitable in growing systems. Managing them well requires versioning discipline, clear communication, incremental migration, and robust testing. Treat breaking changes as team events, not solo refactors.

data.title: Key Takeaways
text: Follow semantic versioning for clear impact signaling
Deprecate before removing; give consumers time to migrate
Document rollback plans and test both old and new behavior
